## Abstract & Guideline Intent

**Purpose:**

1. Identify individuals who may benefit from cancer risk assessment and genetic counseling/testing
2. Guide decisions related to genetic testing
3. Facilitate multidisciplinary care for hereditary colorectal, endometrial, and gastric cancer

**Key Updates:**

- Screening and management of EC in Lynch syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS), and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS)
- Role of multigene panel testing (MGPT)
- **De-implementation of colon cancer screening in individuals with CHEK2 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants**

---

## Overview of Hereditary Cancer Risk

- Hereditary cancers characterized by pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants
- Increased risk for specific cancers; transmitted through mother and/or father
- Often early age of onset; autosomal dominant inheritance
- **All individuals suspected of hereditary cancer risk should be offered genetic counseling**
- Assessment based on thorough personal and family history evaluation

**Syndromes covered:**

- Lynch syndrome (LS)
- Adenomatous polyposis syndromes (FAP, AFAP, MAP)
- Hamartomatous polyposis syndromes (JPS, PJS, PHTS)

---

## Endometrial Cancer Epidemiology

- Most common malignancy of the female genital tract in the United States
- **Estimated 67,880 new cases in 2024; 13,250 deaths**
- \>600,000 survivors of EC in the United States
- **~5% of EC cases attributed to a hereditary syndrome**
  - Lynch syndrome
  - PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS)
  - Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS)
- MGPT has revealed other genes potentially associated with increased EC risk: **BRCA1/2, POLD1, POLE**

---

## Multigene Panel Testing (MGPT) — Definition

**Next-generation sequencing (NGS)** allows simultaneous sequencing of multiple genes.

**Panel Types:**

- **Syndrome-specific:** Multiple genes associated with one syndrome (e.g., LS)
- **Cancer-specific:** Multiple genes associated with one cancer type (e.g., EC)
- **Comprehensive cancer panels:** Many genes associated with multiple cancers/syndromes

**Penetrance inclusion:**

- High-penetrance genes
- High- and moderate-penetrance genes
- Genes with emerging evidence

---

## MGPT — Clinical Rationale

- Identify clinically actionable P/LP variants that alter patient management
- Most useful when >1 gene could explain clinical/family history
- May detect P/LP variants not found with single-gene testing
- Comparable or higher yield for LS compared with tumor-based testing
- May be considered when:
  - Previous limited testing was negative but history strongly suggests inherited susceptibility
  - Individual meets criteria but had absent deletion/duplication analysis
  - More than one P/LP variant could influence condition

---

## MGPT — Advantages

- **Efficiency:** More efficient than sequential single-syndrome testing when multiple genes may explain presentation
- **Yield:** Higher detection rate for LS and other cancer risk genes
- **Actionability:** Identifies variants that inform screening, surveillance, and treatment
- **Cascade testing:** Allows family cascade testing and early detection/prevention opportunities
- **Simplification:** May simplify referral and testing; not entirely dependent on family history or tumor characteristics
- **Reproductive planning:** Can identify carrier status for recessive disorders in offspring

---

## MGPT — Limitations & Challenges

- **VUS:** Increases likelihood of variants of uncertain significance (VUS)
  - 29–63% of individuals with CRC may have a VUS depending on panel size
  - Higher VUS rates in racial/ethnic minority groups
- **Uncertain management:** Some P/LP variants lack clear management guidelines
- **Overtreatment risk:** Potential for overtreatment/overscreening due to uncertain findings
- **Capacity:** Uncertain capacity to deliver pre/post-test counseling to all patients
  - Current genetic testing rates among EC patients: ~6.4%
- **Turnaround time:** Longer turnaround may not suit urgent surgical decision-making
- **Germline alone does NOT inform EC treatment decisions** (tumor MMR testing required for immunotherapy eligibility)

---

## MGPT for Endometrial Cancer — Detection Rates

- MGPT identifies a P/LP variant in **9.2% to 14.7%** of patients with EC
- Unselected populations yield lower positive rates than those selected by personal/family history
- **Cancer risk genes other than LS genes found in 3.4% to 11.8%** of patients with EC
- One prospective study showed **34.5% of LS patients would not have been identified without MGPT**
  - 6 patients had no MSI/IHC performed
  - 4 had tumor findings that would not have triggered germline testing

---

**Key non-LS genes identified:**

- **CHEK2, BRCA1/2, BRIP1, PALB2, RAD51C, ATM, APC, MUTYH** (biallelic), **PTEN, TP53**
- Moderate/low penetrance: **CHEK2, RAD50, NBN**
- Recessive: **MUTYH, MSH3, NTHL1**

---

## MGPT for EC — Histology & Clinical Correlations

- **Limited evidence** for endometrial tumor histology as predictor of non-LS P/LP variants
- Patients with non-LS P/LP variants more likely to have **serous histology** (23% vs 6%; P=.02)
  - Mutations in **BRCA2, BRIP1, RAD51C** observed in serous cases
  
  
---

## MGPT for EC — Histology & Clinical Correlations

- **39% of non-LS P/LP variants** were of non-endometrioid histology
- P/LP variant distribution by histology:
  - Endometrioid: 13.4%
  - Serous: 8.7%
  - Clear cell: 23.9%
  - Carcinosarcoma: 11.3%
  - De-/undifferentiated: 15.2%
  - Mixed/high-grade NOS: 14.5%
- **Age of diagnosis was NOT associated** with greater likelihood of testing positive

---

## MGPT — Minimum Gene Recommendations for EC

**Germline MGPT should include at minimum:**

- **MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM**
- **PTEN**
- **BRCA1, BRCA2**

**May also be considered:**

- **POLD1**
- **POLE**

---

## MGPT — Minimum Gene Recommendations for EC


**Selection/retesting decisions based on:**

- Age at presentation
- Personal and family history of cancer
- Patient and provider preference

---

## NCCN Panel Stance on Upfront MGPT for EC

- **Optimal approach remains uncertain**
- Panel does **not** assert MGPT is logistically simpler than selection based on history + tumor screening
- **Lack of evidence** regarding impact of MGPT on:
  - EC incidence and mortality
  - Inequities in genetic evaluation by race, ethnicity, social determinants
- **Recommendation (Category 2B):** Consider germline MGPT for patients with EC aged ≥50 years who do not meet other testing criteria, based on comprehensive assessment
- **Ideally offered with professional genetic expertise** (pre- and post-test counseling)

---

## HRS-1 — General Criteria: Testing Clinically Indicated

- Any blood relative with a known P/LP variant in a cancer susceptibility gene
- Individuals meeting criteria below who tested negative with previous limited testing and are interested in multigene testing
- P/LP variant identified on tumor genomic testing with clinical implications if also in germline
- Individual meeting LS testing criteria (HRS-3) based on:
  - Family history of LS-associated P/LP variant
  - Personal/family history of LS-related cancer
  - Personal history of dMMR tumor
  
---

## HRS-1 — General Criteria: Testing Clinically Indicated


- Individual meeting adenomatous polyposis testing criteria (POLYP-1)
- Individual meeting clinical criteria for JPS (JPS-1), PJS (PJS-1), HDGC (HGAST-1)
- Individual meeting LFS or CS/PHTS testing criteria

---

## HRS-1 — Genetic Evaluation Clinically Indicated

- **Personal or family history of:**
  - Colorectal cancer (CRC) — see HRS-3
  - Endometrial cancer (EC) — see HRS-3
  - Gastric cancer — see HGAST-1
- Individual meeting clinical criteria for serrated polyposis syndrome (SPS-1)
- **To aid in surgical decision-making:**
  - \>10 adenomatous polyps
  - \>2 hamartomatous polyps
  - \>5 serrated polyps/lesions proximal to the rectum

---

## Lynch Syndrome — Overview

- Accounts for **~3% of all EC cases**
- Results from germline P/LP variant in 1 of 4 DNA MMR genes:
  - **MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2**
- **EPCAM** deletions cause MSH2 silencing → LS
- Autosomal dominant; high penetrance
- **Importance:** High personal risk for metachronous LS cancers; familial implications
- EC is the **second most common LS-associated cancer** in those at risk

---

## Lynch Syndrome — EC Risk by Gene

Lifetime EC risk (through age 80) varies by mutated gene:

| Gene | Average Age of Onset | Cumulative Risk (Age 80) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **MLH1** | ~49 years | 34%–54% |
| **MSH2** | ~49–50 years | 37%–54% |
| **MSH6** | ~55 years | 22%–40% |
| **PMS2** | ~49–50 years | 13%–26% |
| **EPCAM** | Variable | Variable (depends on deletion extent) |

- Individuals with LS (AFAB): lifetime risk up to **60%** for EC

---

## Lynch Syndrome — Testing Strategy Options

**If colorectal or endometrial tumor is available:**

1. **Tumor testing:** IHC or MSI; or comprehensive tumor NGS panel (minimum: 4 MMR genes + EPCAM, BRAF [CRC only], MSI, other familial cancer genes)
2. **Germline MGPT:** Includes at least 4 MMR genes + EPCAM

**Primary approach for pathology lab–based universal screening:** Tumor testing with IHC and/or MSI

**If no tumor available, insufficient material, or affected relative unavailable:**

- Germline MGPT may be considered

**MGPT recommended for:** Patients diagnosed with EC or CRC aged <50 years or with strong family history

---

## HRS-3 — LS Testing Criteria (Personal History)

**Testing clinically indicated for personal history of LS-related cancer (CRC, EC, or other) with ANY of:**

- Diagnosed **<50 years**
- A **synchronous or metachronous** LS-related cancer regardless of age
- **1 first-degree or second-degree relative** with LS-related cancer diagnosed <50 years
- **≥2 first-degree or second-degree relatives** with LS-related cancer regardless of age

**Or increased model-predicted risk:**

- **≥5% risk** of MMR gene P/LP variant by predictive models (PREMM5, MMRpro, MMRpredict)
- PREMM5 score **≥2.5%** with personal history of CRC/EC (increased sensitivity, decreased specificity)

---

## HRS-3 — LS Testing Criteria (Family History & Tumor)

**Family history criteria:**

- ≥1 first-degree relative with CRC or EC diagnosed <50 years
- ≥1 first-degree relative with CRC or EC + synchronous/metachronous LS-related cancer regardless of age
- ≥2 first- or second-degree relatives with LS-related cancers, including ≥1 diagnosed <50 years
- ≥3 first- or second-degree relatives with LS-related cancers regardless of age


---

## HRS-3 — LS Testing Criteria (Family History & Tumor)

**Tumor-based criteria:**

- Personal history of CRC, EC, or other tumor with MMR deficiency by PCR, NGS, or IHC at any age
- Personal history of P/LP variant identified on tumor genomic testing with clinical implications if germline

**May be considered:** Personal history of CRC or EC at age ≥50 years + untested for MMR deficiency or absence of MMR deficiency (Category 2B)

---

## LS Tumor Testing — Differential Diagnosis

**If abnormal MSI or IHC identified in CRC or EC:**

- Differential diagnosis required
- **Absent MSH2 expression by IHC:** Direct germline testing indicated
- **Absent MLH1 expression by IHC (endometrial tumors):**
  - Recommend additional tumor testing for **MLH1 hypermethylation**
  - If hypermethylation present → consistent with **sporadic** (not LS-associated) cancer
  - If no hypermethylation → consider germline testing
- Algorithm (LS-1, LS-A) available at NCCN.org for full result scenarios and follow-up

---

## LS-B — MLH1: Endometrial Cancer Management

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Education & Symptom Recognition:**

- Prompt reporting of dysfunctional uterine bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding
- Evaluation must include **endometrial biopsy**


:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Screening:**

- Endometrial biopsy every **1–2 years** starting at age **30–35 years** may be considered
- Transvaginal ultrasound **not recommended** in premenopausal; may consider in postmenopausal at clinician discretion

:::
:::

**Risk-Reducing Surgery:**

- Total hysterectomy **+ bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO)** may be considered starting at age **40 years**
- Coordinate with colorectal surgery if indicated
- Estrogen replacement therapy should be considered after premature menopause

---

## LS-B — MLH1: Ovarian & Upper GI Surveillance

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Ovarian Cancer:**

- BSO reduces incidence; timing individualized by childbearing status, menopause, comorbidities, family history, gene
- **No routine ovarian cancer screening** (CA-125/TVUS for preoperative planning only)
- **Salpingectomy** option for premenopausal patients not ready for oophorectomy
- Consider risk-reduction agents (oral contraceptives, progestin IUD)

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Gastric & Small Bowel Cancer:**

- Upper GI surveillance with **high-quality EGD starting age 30–40 years**, repeat every **2–4 years**
- Random biopsy of proximal and distal stomach at initial procedure for H. pylori, autoimmune gastritis, intestinal metaplasia
- Push enteroscopy may enhance small bowel visualization
- One-time noninvasive H. pylori testing if not undergoing endoscopic surveillance

:::
:::



---

## LS-C — MSH2: Endometrial & Ovarian Management


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Endometrial Cancer:**

- Education on abnormal bleeding; endometrial biopsy for evaluation
- Hysterectomy + BSO may be considered starting at age **40 years** (higher risks of early EC and ovarian cancer)
- Endometrial biopsy screening every **1–2 years** from age **30–35 years** may be considered
- Transvaginal ultrasound not recommended premenopausal; may consider postmenopausal

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Ovarian Cancer:**

- BSO as risk-reducing option; starting age **40 years** for MSH2
- No routine screening; salpingectomy option for premenopausal patients
- Consider oral contraceptives and progestin IUDs for risk reduction
- Estrogen replacement after premature menopause

:::
:::



---

## LS-C — MSH2/EPCAM: Upper GI & Special Considerations


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Gastric & Small Bowel:**

- EGD starting **30–40 years**, every **2–4 years** (preferably with colonoscopy)
- Earlier initiation (<30 years) or shorter interval (<2 years) based on family history or high-risk findings (GIM, adenomas, Barrett esophagus with dysplasia)
- Random gastric biopsies at initial EGD; H. pylori test/treat

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**EPCAM-Specific Notes:**

- Evidence for gynecologic cancer surveillance recommendations **lacking**
- Cancer risks historically characterized similarly to MSH2, but EC risk is **variable**
- Risk related to extent/location of deletion and proximity to MSH2 promoter
- Currently: counseling and surveillance based on **family history and shared decision-making**
- Risk-reducing surgery may be considered at later age, similar to **PMS2** guidelines

:::
:::



---

## LS-D — MSH6: Endometrial Management

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="55%"}
**Endometrial Cancer:**

- Education on abnormal bleeding; endometrial biopsy for symptoms
- **Hysterectomy with opportunistic bilateral salpingectomy** may be considered starting at age **40 years**
- **Delayed bilateral oophorectomy** starting at age **50 years**
- Endometrial biopsy every **1–2 years** starting at age **30–35 years** may be considered
- Transvaginal ultrasound not recommended premenopausal; may consider postmenopausal

:::

:::{.column width="45%"}
**Rationale for delayed oophorectomy:**

- MSH6 carriers have lower ovarian cancer risk than MLH1/MSH2
- Opportunistic salpingectomy = elective removal of fallopian tubes during other abdominal surgery to prevent tube/ovary/peritoneum cancer

:::
:::



---

## LS-D — MSH6: Ovarian & Upper GI Management


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Ovarian Cancer:**

- **Insufficient evidence** for specific RRSO recommendation in MSH6 carriers
- BSO may reduce incidence; decision individualized
- Salpingectomy at age 40 with delayed oophorectomy at 50
- No routine screening; salpingectomy option for premenopausal patients
- Consider risk-reduction agents (OCP, progestin IUD)
- Estrogen replacement after premature menopause

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Gastric & Small Bowel:**

- EGD starting **30–40 years**, every **2–4 years** with colonoscopy
- Earlier/shorter intervals based on family history or high-risk endoscopic findings
- Random gastric biopsies at initial EGD; H. pylori test/treat


:::
:::


---

## LS-E — PMS2: Endometrial Cancer Surveillance

**Key distinction:** PMS2 carriers at **only modestly increased risk** of EC compared to MLH1, MSH2, MSH6

**Management:**

- Education on abnormal bleeding; endometrial biopsy for evaluation
- **Hysterectomy with BSO may be considered starting at age 50 years**
- Endometrial biopsy every **1–2 years** starting at age **30–35 years** may be considered
- Transvaginal ultrasound not recommended premenopausal; may consider postmenopausal

**Lower risk profile** reflects less aggressive gynecologic cancer risk; surgery deferred to later age than MLH1/MSH2

---

## LS-E — PMS2: Ovarian & Urothelial Considerations

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Ovarian Cancer:**

- **Insufficient evidence** for specific RRSO recommendation
- PMS2 carriers appear at **no greater than average risk** for ovarian cancer
- May reasonably elect **not to have oophorectomy** or defer surveillance
- If BSO chosen, may consider starting at age **50 years**
- Salpingectomy option for premenopausal patients
- Consider risk-reduction agents

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Urothelial Cancer (Renal Pelvis, Ureter, Bladder):**

- **No clear evidence** to support surveillance
- May consider in selected individuals with family history
- Options: annual urinalysis starting at age **30–35 years**
- Insufficient evidence to recommend particular strategy

:::
:::



---

## LS — Hormonal Risk Reduction & Shared Decision-Making

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Hormonal Contraceptives:**

- Observational study: hormonal contraceptive use associated with **lower EC risk** in MMR carriers (HR 0.39; 95% CI 0.23–0.64; P<.001)
- **Prospective data needed** before recommendation for gynecologic cancer prevention
- Risk reduction agents should be considered with detailed discussion of risks/benefits

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**General Principles:**

- Timing of all risk-reducing surgeries individualized based on:
  - Childbearing completion
  - Comorbidities
  - Family history
  - Specific LS gene (risks vary by mutated gene)
- Coordination with colorectal surgery when indicated

:::
:::



---

## Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome — Overview

- **Autosomal dominant** condition characterized by hamartomatous GI polyps
- Increased risk for: CRC, breast, pancreas, stomach, small intestine, lung cancers
- **Gynecologic cancers increased:**
  - Sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT)
  - Endometrial cancer
  - Minimal deviation adenocarcinoma of cervix
- **Testicular cancer:** Sertoli cell tumors
- **STK11/LKB1 mutations** identified in 66–94% of cases
- Detection rate not 100% → suggests possible genetic heterogeneity

---

## PJS — Gynecologic Cancer Surveillance

**Adults:**

- **Pelvic examination and Pap smear:** Annually, beginning ~ages **18–20 years**
- **Annual pelvic ultrasound** may be considered
- **Endometrial biopsy** if abnormal bleeding present
- **Total hysterectomy** (including uterus and cervix) may be considered when childbearing complete

**Children:**

- **Annual physical examination** for observation of precocious puberty beginning ~age **8 years**
- **Annual testicular exam** and observation for feminizing changes beginning ~age **10 years**

---

## PJS-2 — Pediatric Surveillance Recommendations

| Site | Risk/Targets | Screening/Intervention | Initiation Age |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Colon/Stomach** | Bleeding, iron deficiency anemia | Upper endoscopy + high-quality colonoscopy with polypectomy; repeat every 2–3y if polyps found | **8–10 years** |
| **Small intestine** | Bleeding, anemia, intussusception | Video capsule endoscopy or CT/MRI enterography; repeat every 2–3y | **8–10 years** |
| **Ovary** | SCTAT (~20% lifetime risk) | Annual physical for precocious puberty | **~8 years** |
| **Testes** | Sertoli cell tumors (~9% risk) | Annual testicular exam + observation for feminizing changes | **~10 years** |

- Earlier/more frequent if signs/symptoms of GI blood loss or intussusception

---

## PJS-3 — Adult Surveillance: GI Cancers

| Cancer Site | Lifetime Risk | Screening Procedure | Initiation Age |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Colon** | 39% | High-quality colonoscopy every 2–3y | **~18 years** |
| **Stomach** | 29% | Upper endoscopy every 2–3y | **~18 years** |
| **Small intestine** | 13% | VCE or CT/MR enterography every 2–3y | **~18 years** |
| **Pancreas** | 11%–36% | Annual EUS or MRI/MRCP (center of expertise) | **~30–35 years** |

- Shorter intervals indicated based on polyp size, number, and pathology
- Pancreas screening: see also NCCN Guidelines for Breast, Ovarian, and Pancreatic

---

## PJS-3 — Adult Surveillance: Breast & Gynecologic

| Cancer Site | Lifetime Risk | Screening Procedure | Initiation Age |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Breast (female)** | 32%–54% | Mammogram + breast MRI annually; CBE every 6–12mo | **~30 years** |
| **Cervix** | ≥10% | Annual pelvic exam + Pap; consider total hysterectomy after childbearing | **~18–20 years** |
| **Uterus (EC)** | 9% | Annual pelvic exam; endometrial biopsy if abnormal bleeding | **~18–20 years** |
| **Ovary (SCTAT)** | ≥20% | Annual pelvic exam + annual pelvic ultrasound | **~18–20 years** |
| **Testes** | 9% | Annual testicular exam + observation for feminizing changes | Continued from pediatric |
| **Lung** | 7%–17% | Education about symptoms and smoking cessation | N/A |

---

## PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome — Overview

- Spectrum of disorders from germline **PTEN** P/LP variant
- Includes:
  - Cowden syndrome
  - Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome
  - PTEN-related Proteus syndrome
  - Adult Lhermitte-Duclos disease
  - Proteus-like syndrome
  - Autism spectrum disorders with macrocephaly
- **Cowden syndrome incidence:** ~1 in 200,000 (likely underestimated)
- **~80% of Cowden syndrome** cases associated with germline PTEN P/LP variant
- One study: germline **KILLIN methylation** may also be associated

---

## PHTS — Cancer Risks & Endometrial Screening

**Associated lesions:** Hamartomatous and/or cancerous lesions in colon, skin, mucous membranes, breast, thyroid, endometrium, brain

**Endometrial Cancer Risk (AFAB):**

- **5% to 22%** lifetime risk (not well defined)
- Many females have uterine fibroids, but risk not clearly greater than general population


---

## PHTS — Cancer Risks & Endometrial Screening

**Screening Recommendations:**

- **No data on EC screening** in PHTS (rare syndrome)
- Consider screening as early as age **35 years**
- **Patient education** on symptoms (abnormal bleeding) with prompt reporting
- Endometrial biopsy for evaluation of symptoms
- Endometrial biopsy every **1–2 years** may be considered
- Transvaginal ultrasound not recommended premenopausal; may consider postmenopausal

---

## PHTS — Risk-Reducing Surgery Considerations

- **No data** available regarding risk-reducing surgery in PHTS (AFAB)
- Options to discuss:
  - **Risk-reducing mastectomy**
  - **Hysterectomy**
- **Oophorectomy is NOT specifically recommended**
- Counseling should include:
  - Extent of cancer risk reduction/protection
  - Risks associated with surgeries
  - Reproductive options
- **Psychosocial and quality-of-life aspects** must be addressed

---

## POLD1/POLE — Overview & EC Risk

- Primarily associated with **colonic polyposis** and increased CRC risk
- **Limited evidence** for increased extracolonic cancer risk including EC


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Key Studies:**

- 2022 study: 9/17 (53%) with POLD1 exonuclease domain variant had EC; 5/43 (12%) with POLE exonuclease domain variant had EC
- 2023 systematic review & meta-analysis: 11/20 (55%) POLD1 carriers had EC; 11/41 (27%) POLE carriers had EC

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Panel Assessment:**

- Small sample sizes limit evidence
- **Currently insufficient evidence** to support risk management strategies for extracolonic cancers including EC
- NCCN colon cancer risk management recommendations available for these variants

:::
:::



---

## GENE-11 — POLD1: Detailed Management

| Feature | Recommendation |
|:---|:---|
| **Syndrome** | Polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis (PPAP) |
| **Estimated absolute CRC risk** | >20% |
| **Colonoscopy** | Begin age 25–30y (or 2–5y prior to earliest CRC if <25y); repeat every 2–3y if negative |
| **If polyps found** | Colonoscopy every 1–2y; surgical evaluation if polyp burden unmanageable |
| **Colorectal phenotype** | 30–100 adenomas |
| **Other cancers** | EC, breast, brain, possibly others (limited evidence) |
| **Key molecular note** | Gain-of-function P/LP in exonuclease domain (aa 304–533) = PPAP; LOF/outside domain = MDPL syndrome |

---

## GENE-11 — POLE: Detailed Management

| Feature | Recommendation |
|:---|:---|
| **Syndrome** | Polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis (PPAP) |
| **Estimated absolute CRC risk** | >20% |
| **Colonoscopy** | Begin age 25–30y (or 2–5y prior to earliest CRC if <25y); repeat every 2–3y if negative |
| **If polyps found** | Colonoscopy every 1–2y; surgical evaluation if polyp burden unmanageable |
| **Colorectal phenotype** | 30–100 adenomas |
| **Other cancers** | Colon, endometrial, ovarian, brain, extracolonic GI; limited evidence for breast, melanoma |
| **Key molecular note** | Gain-of-function in exonuclease domain (aa 268–471, exons 9–14) = PPAP; LOF/outside = FILS / IMAGE-1 syndromes |

---

## BRCA1/2 — Endometrial Cancer Risk

- Widely accepted as highly penetrant for **breast and ovarian cancer**
- Also associated with pancreas and prostate cancer
- **Some studies suggest increased risk of serous uterine cancer**

**Key Evidence:**

- Multicenter prospective cohort (1,083 BRCA1 carriers after RRSO without hysterectomy): increased risk for serous/serous-like EC
- Dutch cohort (5,980 BRCA1/2 carriers): **2- to 3-fold increased risk** for EC; highest for serous-like (HR 10.48) and p53-abnormal (HR 15.71) in BRCA1
- Meta-analysis (11 studies, 13,871 patients): EC prevalence 0.62% BRCA1, 0.47% BRCA2
- Uterine papillary serous carcinoma: 0.20% BRCA1, 0.08% BRCA2

---

## BRCA1/2 — Management & Tamoxifen Consideration

**Risk Attribution:**

- Increased EC risk observed in some patients may be due to **tamoxifen therapy** rather than P/LP variant alone
- Absolute risk of uterine cancer appears **low overall** despite evidence of increased risk

**Management:**

- Information on gynecologic cancer management in BRCA1/2 carriers found in:
  - **NCCN Guidelines for Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Breast, Ovarian, and Pancreatic**
- No specific EC screening recommendations in this colorectal/endometrial guideline

---

## CHEK2 — Background & Early Evidence

- Germline P/LP variants in **CHEK2** associated with increased **breast cancer** risk
- Association with **CRC risk historically uncertain**

**Early Meta-Analyses (≤2012):**

- Significant associations identified between CHEK2 variants and CRC risk
- CHEK2 I157T variant: significant association with CRC
- CHEK2 1100delC variant: strong cumulative evidence (OR 1.88; P=.001)

**Reanalysis:**

- Corrected data from one included study showed **1100delC NOT significantly associated** with CRC risk in familial or sporadic subgroups
- Larger unselected CRC group showed **reduction in overall CRC risk** in carriers

---

## CHEK2 — Recent Cohort Evidence

**2022 Retrospective Cohort (3,783 patients with CHEK2 P/LP):**

- CHEK2 **NOT associated with CRC**
- Carriers **less likely** to be diagnosed with CRC (OR 0.62; P<.001)
- Similar result for 1100delC specifically (OR 0.69; P=.002)

**Second Large Retrospective Study (6,255 carriers):**

- No significant difference in CRC prevalence among truncating (2.2%) or missense (1.8%) carriers vs. non-carriers (2.2%)

**ACMG Clinical Practice Resource (2023):**

- Published data at best supportive of **moderate association**
- Risk falls below level defined as **low increased risk**
- Earlier screening model based on old data; not supported by newer large cohorts

---

## CHEK2 — NCCN De-Implementation Recommendation


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**For patients with CHEK2 P/LP variant:**

- **Screening and surveillance per general population guidelines**
  - NCCN Guidelines for Colon Cancer
  - NCCN Guidelines for Rectal Cancer
  - NCCN Guidelines for Colorectal Cancer Screening

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Specific Recommendation:**

- For patients **unaffected by CRC** and **without a first-degree relative with CRC:**
  - **General population screening is appropriate**

**Rationale:**

- Lack of significant association between CHEK2 P/LP variants and CRC risk in recent large studies
- Avoid unnecessary intensive screening and patient anxiety

:::
:::



---

## GENE-6 — CHEK2: Risk & Management Summary

| Feature | Recommendation |
|:---|:---|
| **Estimated absolute CRC risk** | **No increased risk** |
| **Management (average risk)** | **General population screening** |
| **Management (personal or 1° family history of CRC/polyps)** | Increased screening per NCCN Colon/Rectal/Colorectal Screening Guidelines |
| **Strength of evidence** | **Strong** |
| **Colorectal phenotype** | No polyposis |
| **Other cancers** | Increased lifetime risk of breast cancer |
| **Breast cancer management** | Per NCCN Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Breast, Ovarian, and Pancreatic |

## Multigene Testing — Overview (GENE-1)

- NGS-based tests simultaneously analyze genes associated with specific or multiple phenotypes
- **More efficient** than single-gene testing when >1 gene may explain presentation
- Role for individuals who tested negative for single syndrome but history strongly suggests inherited susceptibility
- **Chances of VUS or uncertain PV increase** as number of genes increases
- **VUS reclassification is commonplace:** Historically >91% of VUS downgraded to benign/likely benign
- Clinical phenotypic correlation warranted; discuss with laboratory if evidence supports pathogenicity

**Test selection important:** Commercial tests differ in genes analyzed, variant classification, reclassification procedures, turnaround time, and insurance coverage

---

## Table 1 — Multigene Testing Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Multigene panel** | Laboratory test including >1 gene |
| **Syndrome-specific panel** | Tests multiple genes for one syndrome only (e.g., LS) |
| **Cancer-specific panel** | Tests multiple genes associated with one cancer type |
| **"Comprehensive" cancer panel** | Tests multiple genes associated with multiple cancers/syndromes |
| **Actionable pathogenic variant** | Results in recommendation for change in clinical management |
| **Variant of uncertain significance (VUS)** | Sequence variant of uncertain significance; generally not actionable; most ultimately reclassified as benign |

---

## Table 2 — Pros and Cons of Multigene Testing

| Pros | Cons |
|:---|:---|
| More efficient when multiple genes may explain presentation | Higher chance of PVs with uncertain clinical management (~3–4%) |
| Higher chance of providing explanation for cancer cause | Higher chance of VUS (17–38%) |
| Competitive cost vs. sequential single-gene testing | Higher chance of overtreatment/overscreening if VUS/uncertain PVs misinterpreted |
| Identifies PVs in multiple actionable genes missed by syndrome-specific panels | — |

---

## HRS-A 1/3 — Rationale for MGPT in LS

**Rationale:**

- Germline MGPT is an **alternative** to tumor- and family history-driven selection
- **More sensitive** for identifying individuals with LS and other cancer risk genes than selection based on history/tumor criteria alone

**Why consider MGPT?**

- Majority of individuals with personal history of CRC or EC **do not meet** previous NCCN criteria based on family history or tumor-based criteria alone
- MGPT may simplify referral and testing
- Not entirely dependent on family history or tumor characteristics
- Steps for evaluating genetic syndrome are simplified

---

## HRS-A 1/3 — Pros of MGPT

| Advantage | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **LS yield** | Comparable or higher than tumor-/history-based strategies |
| **Other gene yield** | 7.8%–16.0% PV in CRC; 9.2%–14.7% PV in EC |
| **Actionability** | Some PVs inform screening and surveillance |
| **Cascade testing** | Allows family testing and early detection/prevention |
| **Sensitivity** | Identifies patients who would not meet traditional criteria |
| **Simplification** | May simplify referral and testing workflow |

---

## HRS-A 1/3 — Cons of MGPT

| Limitation | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **Treatment decisions** | Germline result alone does NOT inform CRC/EC treatment; tumor MSI/IHC required for immunotherapy |
| **Uncertain PVs** | PVs in genes with uncertain clinical management will be identified |
| **VUS burden** | 29%–63% of CRC patients may have VUS depending on panel size |
| **Health equity** | Higher VUS rates in racial/ethnic minorities; propagates inequities |
| **Capacity** | Uncertain capacity to counsel all patients (150,000 CRC + 66,200 EC annually) |
| **Timing** | Results may not return in time for surgical decision-making |

---

## HRS-A 2/3 — Challenges & Evidence Gaps

| Challenge | Detail |
|:---|:---|
| **Cascade testing impact** | Uncertain; reported in only 16%–65% of families |
| **Cost effectiveness** | Uncertain; no recent U.S.-based study using current costs |
| **Unselected yield** | Yield in CRC unselected by other characteristics uncertain |
| **Selection bias** | Most studies have potential bias that may overestimate yield |
| **Racial/ethnic spectrum** | Spectrum of PVs in diverse populations requires additional research |

**Swiss study suggested MGPT cost-effective relative to tumor-based LS screening, but U.S. data lacking**

---

## HRS-A 2/3 — Test Selection: CRC Panels

**Minimum genes for CRC/polyposis risk:**

- **APC, BMPR1A, EPCAM, MUTYH, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, PTEN, SMAD4, STK11, TP53**

**May also be considered:**

- Monoallelic PVs: **AXIN2, GREM1, POLE, POLD1**
- Biallelic PVs: **MSH3, MLH3, MBD4, NTHL1**

**Additional genes on some panels:**

- ATM, BLM, CHEK2, FOCAD, GALNT12, RNF43, RPS20

---

## HRS-A 2/3 — Test Selection: EC Panels

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Minimum genes for EC risk:**

- **MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM**
- **PTEN**
- **BRCA1, BRCA2**

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**May also be considered:**

- **POLD1**
- **POLE**

:::
:::



**Selection/retesting beyond minimum sets based on:**

- Age at presentation
- Polyp phenotype
- Personal and family history
- Patient and provider preference

---

## Summary — Key Takeaways on MGPT & EC

1. **MGPT identifies P/LP variants in 9–15% of EC patients**, with higher yields in high-risk cohorts
2. **Minimum EC panel genes:** MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, PTEN, BRCA1/2
3. **POLD1/POLE** may be considered but extracolonic management evidence is insufficient
4. **VUS rates are significant** (especially in minority populations) and require expert counseling
5. **Germline MGPT alone does NOT guide immunotherapy decisions** — tumor MMR testing required
6. **Optimal upfront MGPT approach remains uncertain** — shared decision-making recommended

---

## Summary — Syndrome-Specific EC Management

| Syndrome | Key EC Risk Management |
|:---|:---|
| **Lynch (MLH1/MSH2)** | Consider hysterectomy + BSO starting age **40y**; endometrial biopsy every 1–2y from 30–35y |
| **Lynch (MSH6)** | Hysterectomy + salpingectomy at **40y**; delayed oophorectomy at **50y** |
| **Lynch (PMS2)** | Hysterectomy + BSO may be considered starting **50y**; lower risk profile |
| **Lynch (EPCAM)** | Manage based on **family history**; later surgery similar to PMS2 |
| **PJS** | Annual pelvic exam + Pap from 18–20y; endometrial biopsy if bleeding; hysterectomy after childbearing |
| **PHTS** | Consider endometrial biopsy every 1–2y from **35y**; educate on bleeding symptoms |

---

## Summary — CHEK2 & Colorectal De-Implementation

- **CHEK2 P/LP variants:** No longer considered to confer significantly increased CRC risk
- **Recommendation:** General population CRC screening for unaffected carriers without first-degree family history
- **Rationale based on:**
  - Large retrospective cohorts showing no association
  - ACMG review concluding risk below "low increased risk" threshold
  - Older screening models invalidated by newer data

**Clinical action:** Remove CHEK2 from high-risk colorectal surveillance protocols; redirect to average-risk guidelines
